session.evaluation_method: Automated analysis of NEON API metadata and schema.org JSON-LD

dataset.title: Ground beetles sampled from pitfall traps
dataset.citation: NEON (National Ecological Observatory Network). Ground beetles sampled from pitfall traps (DP1.10022.001), provisional data. Dataset accessed from https://data.neonscience.org/data-products/DP1.10022.001 on January 26, 2026.

evaluator.name: Automated FAIR4AI Evaluation
evaluator.evaluation_description: Evaluating the dataset using NEON API metadata (JSON) and schema.org JSON-LD metadata extracted from the product page.

responses.question: The full citation is provided, preferably in BibTeX format.
responses.evidence: Citation is provided in schema.org metadata but not in BibTeX format.
responses.recommendation: Provide a BibTeX-formatted citation in the dataset metadata or landing page to support direct import into reference managers.

responses.question: Summary or abstract is provided.
responses.evidence: productAbstract and productDescription fields provide a comprehensive description covering sampling methods, processing, identification procedures, and data latency.

responses.question: Publisher is identified.
responses.evidence: NEON (National Ecological Observatory Network) identified in schema.org metadata as publisher. Publisher URL: https://data.neonscience.org

responses.question: Date created is provided.
responses.evidence: Temporal coverage spans 2013-07 to 2025-12 with detailed change logs showing issue and resolution dates. Initial data collection started in 2013.

responses.question: The dataset has a unique, persistent, machine-resolvable identifier (e.g., DOI).
responses.evidence: Product identifier DP1.10022.001 and persistent URL provided, but no DOI. URL: https://data.neonscience.org/data-products/DP1.10022.001
responses.notes: NEON product IDs are stable but not globally resolvable outside NEON infrastructure.
responses.recommendation: Register a DOI for each versioned release through a data repository such as Zenodo or the NEON data portal to provide a globally resolvable, citable identifier.

responses.question: Author/creator information is provided (names, affiliations, ORCIDs).
responses.evidence: No individual author names, affiliations, or ORCIDs provided. NEON listed as organizational creator only.
responses.recommendation: Add individual contributor names and ORCIDs for data collectors, processors, and curators. Use the DataCite contributor roles (DataCollector, DataCurator, etc.) to distinguish roles.

responses.question: Curator information is provided (names, ORCIDs).
responses.evidence: Science team (Terrestrial Observation System - TOS) is identified, but no individual curator names or ORCIDs. External taxonomists at CMNH and ESSIG mentioned but not individually named.
responses.recommendation: Name individual curators and external taxonomists in the metadata with ORCIDs where available. This is especially important for taxonomic annotations, which are a form of expert labeling for AI use.

responses.question: Dataset card author(s) are identified (who wrote the dataset description).
responses.evidence: No specific dataset card authors identified. Organizational attribution to NEON only.
responses.recommendation: Designate and name the individual(s) responsible for the dataset documentation so users know who to credit and who can answer documentation questions.

responses.question: A contact person or expert contact is provided for dataset questions.
responses.evidence: No specific contact person or email provided in metadata. Only organization URL provided.
responses.recommendation: Add a direct contact email or named contact person to the metadata. For large institutional datasets, a group inbox (e.g., neon-data-support@...) is sufficient.

responses.question: Non-author contributions are acknowledged.
responses.evidence: Field technicians, parataxonomists, and expert taxonomists (CMNH, ESSIG) mentioned in the workflow description.
responses.notes: Contributions described at the role level but not attributed to specific individuals.

responses.question: Funding description and grant numbers are provided.
responses.evidence: No funding information or grant numbers provided in the metadata. NEON is NSF-funded but this is not documented.
responses.recommendation: Add NSF award numbers and funder information to dataset metadata using the DataCite fundingReferences or schema.org funder fields.

responses.question: Is this dataset derived from other sources?
responses.evidence: This is primary observational data collected through field sampling with processing (sorting, identification) but not derived from other datasets.

responses.question: Provenance tracking: metadata provide information about the source data (titles, summaries, links).
responses.evidence: Not a derived dataset.

responses.question: Source data producers are identified.
responses.evidence: Not a derived dataset.

responses.question: Citations for subsumed datasets are provided.
responses.evidence: Not a derived dataset.

responses.question: Source data DOIs or permalinks are provided.
responses.evidence: Not a derived dataset.

responses.question: Source data checksums are provided to ensure downstream users obtain the same data.
responses.evidence: Not a derived dataset.

responses.question: Is there additional provenance information not captured above?
responses.evidence: The metadata includes extensive change logs documenting modifications to sampling design, processing pipelines, and data quality issues over time. Biorepository collections documented with DarwinCore Archive links.

responses.question: Related paper(s) are referenced (DOI, BibTeX citation, or link).
responses.evidence: No peer-reviewed publications referenced in the metadata. Protocol documents are provided but are not peer-reviewed.
responses.recommendation: Link any peer-reviewed publications that describe or have used this dataset, providing DOIs. Consider adding a 'cited by' list as the dataset accumulates literature use.

responses.question: Related datasets and/or models are referenced.
responses.evidence: Biorepository collections linked with DarwinCore Archive downloads for specimen data. Ten biorepository collections referenced (NEON-CARC-AP, NEON-CARC-DNA, etc.).

responses.question: Purpose of the data is described.
responses.evidence: Purpose described: sampling ground beetle abundance and diversity at NEON sites for biodiversity monitoring and taxonomic identification.

responses.question: Content is described (short description of data types).
responses.evidence: Comprehensive description of data types: field data, sorting data, taxonomic identifications, archive information. Seven data tables described with expected latency for each.

responses.question: Are the data machine-ready (machine-actionable under the FAIR Principles)?
responses.evidence: Data available via API in JSON format with schema.org structured metadata. FAIR principles supported through structured metadata, persistent identifiers, and programmatic access.

responses.question: Language of the data is documented.
responses.evidence: Language not explicitly stated in metadata. English is used but not formally documented.
responses.recommendation: Add a language field to the metadata (e.g., 'en' per ISO 639-1). This is especially important for text fields such as taxonomic notes, remarks, and quality flag descriptions.

responses.question: Keywords/tags are provided to describe the dataset.
responses.evidence: 22 keywords provided covering taxonomic, methodological, and thematic aspects (diversity, taxonomy, beetles, Carabidae, pitfall traps, biodiversity, etc.).

responses.question: The dataset and its metadata make use of relevant ontologies.
responses.evidence: Uses schema.org ontology for metadata. References taxonomic hierarchies and NEON taxon tables. DarwinCore archives indicate use of biodiversity standards.

responses.question: A data dictionary or codebook is provided.
responses.evidence: Schema.org metadata includes variablesMeasured with 141+ variables listed, but full data dictionary is in separate user guide documents not linked directly from structured metadata.
responses.recommendation: Provide a complete data dictionary as a machine-readable file (e.g., CSV or JSON) linked directly from the dataset metadata, with full field descriptions, allowed values, units, and controlled vocabulary references for all variables.

responses.question: File format(s) that encode the data are documented.
responses.evidence: Data tables implied to be tabular but specific file formats not explicitly stated in structured metadata.
responses.notes: Likely CSV based on NEON standards, but not confirmed in reviewed metadata.
responses.recommendation: Explicitly document file formats in structured metadata using standard encoding format terms (e.g., 'text/csv', 'application/json') mapped to schema.org encodingFormat or DataCite formats.

responses.question: The dataset layout pattern is described.
responses.evidence: Multiple related tables described: bet_fielddata, bet_sorting, bet_parataxonomistID, bet_expertTaxonomistID, bet_archivepooling, bet_identificationHistory. Partitioned by site (47 sites) with documented table relationships.

responses.question: The primary unit of data (record type) is identified.
responses.evidence: One record per trap per collection date (bet_fielddata), with child records for sorting and identification. Hierarchical structure with relationships between tables clearly described.

responses.question: Features or attributes are properly documented in the metadata.
responses.evidence: 141+ variables documented in schema.org metadata with names and units. Includes fields for location, taxonomy, dates, counts, quality flags, and identifiers.

responses.question: Features or attributes are included for each data instance.
responses.evidence: Each record has associated metadata for location, date, taxonomy, and quality flags. Complete metadata described for each trap/specimen record.

responses.question: Technical specifications of the dataset are documented (size, record counts, etc.).
responses.evidence: Sampling specifications provided (trap size, preservative volume, number of traps), but file sizes and total record counts are not documented in metadata.
responses.recommendation: Add digital file specifications to structured metadata: total file sizes, approximate record counts per table, and number of sites/years represented. These help AI/ML users assess computational requirements before downloading.

responses.question: Metadata record what type(s) of source data were collected or used to generate this dataset.
responses.evidence: Field observations and specimens collected via pitfall traps, followed by lab processing and taxonomic identification.

responses.question: Metadata record the primary rationale for curating or assembling this dataset.
responses.evidence: Part of NEON's standardized long-term ecological monitoring program for biodiversity assessment. Quality-controlled, native sampling resolution data for ground beetle abundance and diversity.

responses.question: Metadata indicate if this dataset is part of a larger collection or series.
responses.evidence: Part of NEON Terrestrial Observation System (TOS), collected at all 47 terrestrial NEON sites. Included in NEON Data Product Catalog.

responses.question: Metadata describe the instruments or sensors used to collect the data, including specifications and configuration.
responses.evidence: Pitfall traps described: 16 oz deli containers with 150 or 250 mL propylene glycol. Trap configuration and deployment described (20m from plot center, cardinal directions).

responses.question: Metadata describe the methods used to collect or generate the data.
responses.evidence: Detailed protocol documentation referenced (NEON.DOC.014050). Biweekly sampling during growing season (temperatures >4°C), sorting, pinning, and expert identification procedures described.

responses.question: Metadata describe the spatial resolution.
responses.evidence: Plot-based sampling with trap locations ~20m from plot center. Point locations with coordinates provided for each trap.

responses.question: Metadata describe the geographic coverage (region, bounding box, domain).
responses.evidence: 47 NEON sites across North America with bounding boxes and coordinates for each site. Continental-scale coverage from Alaska to Puerto Rico.

responses.question: Metadata describe the temporal resolution.
responses.evidence: Biweekly sampling during growing season. Event-based sampling with collection dates recorded.

responses.question: Metadata describe the temporal extent.
responses.evidence: 2013-07 to 2025-12 (ongoing). Long-term monitoring program with seasonal sampling.

responses.question: Metadata describe the types of annotations or labels included in the dataset.
responses.evidence: Taxonomic identifications (species/morphospecies), counts, quality flags. Categorical labels for species with hierarchical taxonomy.

responses.question: Metadata describe how annotations were generated or obtained.
responses.evidence: Mixed process: NEON technician parataxonomists perform initial identification; a subset is sent to expert taxonomists for verification. Human expert identification with quality control through expert verification.

responses.question: Metadata indicate who performed the data annotations (names, ORCIDs, or tool versions).
responses.evidence: NEON field technicians and parataxonomists, plus external expert taxonomists (CMNH, ESSIG). Multiple taxonomist SOPs referenced but individual annotator names not provided.
responses.recommendation: Name individual annotators or provide ORCIDs, especially for the expert taxonomist verification step. For AI training purposes, annotation provenance at the individual level is important for assessing label reliability.

responses.question: Is there additional source data information not captured above?
responses.evidence: Sampling design changed over time: 40 traps/site (2013-2017), reduced to 30 traps/site (2018-2022), then 18 traps/site (2023+) due to budget constraints. This is a critical AI/ML consideration for temporal comparisons.

responses.question: Metadata provide a complete description of data preparation, cleaning, transformation, or QC steps performed prior to generating the final dataset.
responses.evidence: Processing described: generic pipeline implemented in 2017, manual QA to rectify mismatches between field samples and downstream tables. Multiple steps documented in change logs.

responses.question: Metadata describe and cite any processing platform or software used in creating this dataset.
responses.evidence: References to 'generic code' and processing pipeline transitions documented (OS_generic_transitions_vA), but specific software tools and versions are not named.
responses.recommendation: Name specific software tools and versions (e.g., R packages, Python libraries) used in the processing pipeline and link to code repositories or DOIs where available.

responses.question: Metadata describe corrections applied to data values and any standardization procedures.
responses.evidence: Taxonomic standardization: higher taxonomy sourced from NEON taxon tables, synonymies reassigned to current valid names. State-level obfuscation applied for sensitive species. Taxonomic determinations archived when updated.

responses.question: Metadata indicate whether missing values or data gaps have been filled.
responses.evidence: samplingImpractical flag added to indicate when data are temporarily missing vs. permanently unavailable. Starting 2020, one record always generated per scheduled trap even if not collected.

responses.question: If gaps were filled, are the methods described?
responses.evidence: Quality flags indicate missing data but gap-filling methods are not described. Missing data is flagged rather than filled/imputed.
responses.recommendation: Explicitly state that missing data is flagged (not imputed) and document all flag values with their meanings in a machine-readable format. For AI/ML users, the distinction between true absence, detection failure, and missing data is critical for model training.

responses.question: Metadata indicate if any labeling or relabeling steps were applied.
responses.evidence: Taxonomic relabeling occurs when expert taxonomists provide updated identifications. Past determinations archived in bet_identificationHistory table when updated.

responses.question: Metadata sufficiently describe the labeling or relabeling process.
responses.evidence: Initial identification by parataxonomists, subset verified by expert taxonomists, updates tracked in identification history. External taxonomist SOPs referenced.

responses.question: Metadata describe whether outlier removal or filtering procedures were applied.
responses.evidence: Quality control procedures mentioned but specific outlier removal methods not described. Manual QA performed but statistical outlier detection methods not documented.
responses.recommendation: Document specific quality control thresholds, rules, or criteria used to flag or remove outliers. Distinguish between manual review decisions and rule-based automated flags.

responses.question: Metadata sufficiently describe the outlier detection and removal methods.
responses.evidence: Quality control mentioned but outlier detection methods not specified. Manual review processes described but not algorithmic approaches.
responses.recommendation: Describe or cite the specific criteria used to identify anomalous records (e.g., count thresholds, geographic impossibilities, phenological outliers). This is especially important for AI/ML users who need to understand data cleaning decisions that could bias training datasets.

responses.question: Metadata indicate if the dataset has been split into training, validation, and/or test sets.
responses.evidence: Observational ecological data not designed for ML train/test splits. No predefined splits exist.
responses.recommendation: Although predefined splits are not expected for primary observational data, consider providing guidance on recommended split strategies for AI/ML use. For example, splitting by site or by year would reduce spatial and temporal data leakage — a known issue when training species distribution or identification models on NEON data.

responses.question: Metadata provide information on how splits were created.
responses.evidence: No predefined splits.

responses.question: Metadata indicate if this dataset is complete (no further updates planned).
responses.evidence: Provisional data; ongoing monitoring program through 2025-12 and beyond. Long-term program with regular updates.
responses.recommendation: Clearly document the dataset's status as an ongoing product with expected update frequency and any plans for a final versioned release.

responses.question: Quality assurance checks have been run and passed.
responses.evidence: Quality-controlled data product. Manual QA performed, expert taxonomist verification for subset of specimens. Multi-level QA: field technicians, parataxonomists, expert taxonomists.

responses.question: Metadata describe the timeliness of the dataset.
responses.evidence: Data latency documented for each table: bet_fielddata: 75 days; bet_sorting/parataxonomistID/archivepooling: 330 days; expert IDs: 600 days.

responses.question: Metadata evaluate timeliness of data relative to the sampling schedule.
responses.evidence: Sampling timing described (biweekly during growing season, >4°C) but formal timeliness QA not described.
responses.recommendation: Document expected vs. actual data delivery timelines and flag cases where delivery significantly exceeded the stated latency.

responses.question: The time lag between data collection and availability is described.
responses.evidence: Specific latency provided: 75-600 days depending on data table. Clear documentation of expected time from collection to publication.

responses.question: Metadata describe quality checks that have failed and provide context for downstream users.
responses.evidence: Change logs document issues and resolutions over time, including mismatches between field and lab data. 12+ issues documented with dates and resolutions.

responses.question: Metadata describe known gaps or limitations in dataset completeness.
responses.evidence: samplingImpractical flag indicates gaps. Change logs document sampling reductions and site closures. COVID-19 impacts, flooding events, and budget-driven sampling reductions documented.

responses.question: Metadata indicate whether all units have been translated into compatible forms.
responses.evidence: Schema.org metadata shows standardized units (meter, decimalDegree, nominalDay). Units provided for measurable variables.

responses.question: Data follow a controlled vocabulary, and a reference is provided for it.
responses.evidence: Taxonomic names follow NEON taxon tables and quality flags use controlled terms. However, NEON taxon tables are referenced but not directly linked in structured metadata.
responses.recommendation: Provide direct URIs to the controlled vocabularies used (e.g., NEON taxon tables, ITIS, Catalogue of Life) in structured metadata so the references are machine-resolvable, not just prose mentions.

responses.question: Metadata describe quality assurance or peer review procedures applied to the dataset.
responses.evidence: Internal quality control by NEON, external expert taxonomist verification for a subset of specimens. Multi-level QA: field technicians, parataxonomists, expert taxonomists.

responses.question: Metadata describe procedures used to ensure data integrity.
responses.evidence: Identification history tracked, data reprocessing documented in change logs. Version control implicit in releases but not explicitly described.
responses.recommendation: Describe the versioning scheme explicitly and publish checksums (e.g., SHA-256) for all released data files to enable downstream integrity verification.

responses.question: The dataset implements checksums for file integrity verification.
responses.evidence: No mention of checksums in metadata.
responses.recommendation: Generate and publish SHA-256 checksums for all released data files. This is especially important for large or frequently updated datasets where users need to verify they have a complete and uncorrupted copy.

responses.question: Metadata describe known sources of bias in the dataset.
responses.evidence: Taxonomic uncertainty acknowledged through expert verification process. Sampling design changes may affect temporal comparisons. Parataxonomist uncertainty estimated through expert re-identification, but broader geographic and detection bias not explicitly discussed.
responses.recommendation: Add an explicit bias section documenting: (1) geographic sampling bias (NEON site selection is not random across all North American biomes), (2) detection probability variation by season, habitat, and trap condition, and (3) parataxonomist vs. expert identification discrepancy rates. These are critical for AI/ML users building species identification or distribution models.

responses.question: Metadata describe known risks or limitations associated with the dataset.
responses.evidence: Limitations documented: reduced sampling effort over time (budget constraints), species obfuscation for conservation, sampling gaps during COVID-19. Change logs provide extensive documentation.

responses.question: Metadata indicate if the dataset is based on experimental data.
responses.evidence: Correctly documented as observational monitoring, not experimental. Standardized sampling design but no treatments or controls.

responses.question: Metadata describe recommended or intended uses of this dataset.
responses.evidence: Purpose described (biodiversity monitoring, abundance and diversity assessment) but specific analytical recommendations not provided in structured metadata. User guide referenced but not included.
responses.recommendation: Add explicit usage guidance to structured metadata, particularly for AI/ML applications: recommended split strategies (site-based or year-based), known confounders to control for (sampling effort changes, seasonal variation), and appropriate downstream tasks (e.g., species richness modeling, occupancy estimation).

responses.question: Metadata describe known inappropriate or discouraged uses of this dataset.
responses.evidence: No explicit guidance on inappropriate uses. Limitations described but not framed as use restrictions.
responses.recommendation: Document use cases that should be avoided, particularly: (1) naive temporal comparisons across sampling design changes (40 → 30 → 18 traps/site), (2) using obfuscated species records for fine-scale distribution modeling, and (3) training ML models on parataxonomist IDs alone without accounting for expert correction rates.

responses.question: Metadata indicate whether this dataset has been used in AI/ML applications previously.
responses.evidence: No mention of ML/AI applications in metadata. Ecological monitoring data, likely not designed for ML.
responses.recommendation: If this dataset has been used in published AI/ML applications, document those uses and link to the papers. Even if not yet used, add a placeholder section to invite reporting of AI/ML use cases — this supports the broader goal of building an AI/ML usage history for the dataset.

responses.question: If used in AI/ML, references to models, benchmarks, or publications are provided.
responses.evidence: No ML references provided.

responses.question: Metadata indicate how to report issues or errors in the dataset.
responses.evidence: No specific contact or issue reporting mechanism in metadata. Organization URL provided but no issue tracker or contact email.
responses.recommendation: Provide a direct issue reporting mechanism in the metadata — a contact email, a GitHub issues URL, or a NEON support portal link. This is a low-cost improvement that significantly aids responsible long-term data stewardship.

responses.question: The dataset is available for direct download.
responses.evidence: Data product available through NEON data portal.

responses.question: The dataset is accessible via an API.
responses.evidence: Metadata accessed via NEON API (https://data.neonscience.org/api/v0/products/DP1.10022.001). RESTful API available.

responses.question: The type of API provided is documented.
responses.evidence: NEON API is RESTful.

responses.question: The dataset is accessible via a cloud platform.
responses.evidence: Not specified in metadata. Cloud availability may exist but is not documented.
responses.recommendation: Document whether data are available via cloud platforms (e.g., AWS Open Data Registry, Google Cloud). Cloud access with standardized formats (e.g., Parquet, Zarr) greatly reduces barriers for large-scale AI/ML workflows.

responses.question: The dataset is provided in a machine-readable format.
responses.evidence: API returns JSON; schema.org structured metadata provided. FAIR-compliant structured metadata.

responses.question: The dataset is provided in an open (non-proprietary) format.
responses.evidence: JSON metadata, CSV data tables (NEON standard). Non-proprietary formats.

responses.question: The dataset is available in multiple formats.
responses.evidence: Basic and expanded data packages available. DarwinCore archives for biorepository specimens. Multiple data product variants.

responses.question: Metadata indicate what license applies to this dataset.
responses.evidence: License URL provided: https://www.neonscience.org/data-samples/data-policies-citation. NEON data policy linked in schema.org metadata.

responses.question: License information is provided in a standardized or machine-readable format.
responses.evidence: License URL included in schema.org JSON-LD, but no SPDX identifier is used.
responses.recommendation: Adopt an SPDX license identifier (e.g., CC-BY-4.0) in the metadata to make the license fully machine-readable and interoperable with AI/ML dataset registries such as Hugging Face and Croissant-compliant catalogs.

responses.question: The dataset contains personal or sensitive information, and this is documented.
responses.evidence: Species of concern have 'fuzzed' taxonomic IDs for conservation. State-level and federal-level obfuscation applied and documented.
responses.notes: Sensitive species information protected; no personal human data.

responses.question: Access restrictions are documented.
responses.evidence: Sensitive species data obfuscated; National Park sites have additional restrictions. Data publicly accessible but some information masked for conservation.
responses.recommendation: Explicitly list which species or sites are subject to obfuscation or access restrictions, and provide the criteria used to determine restriction levels. This allows AI/ML users to anticipate where their models may encounter deliberately degraded location data.

responses.question: Secure access is required to obtain or use the dataset.
responses.evidence: isAccessibleForFree: true in schema.org metadata. Publicly accessible data requiring no authentication.

strengths: Comprehensive structured metadata using schema.org vocabulary
Detailed documentation of methods, protocols, and sampling design
Extensive temporal and spatial coverage (47 sites, 2013-2025)
Multi-level quality control with expert taxonomist verification
Transparent documentation of data quality issues and changes via change logs
Free and open access with clear licensing
Integration with biorepository specimens and DarwinCore archives
Taxonomic relabeling history preserved in identification history table
gaps: No individual author/contributor names or ORCIDs
No direct contact person or issue reporting mechanism
No funding or grant information in metadata
File format specifications not explicitly stated in structured metadata
No checksums for data integrity verification
Specific software/platform names for processing not provided
No guidance on AI/ML-appropriate split strategies given sampling design changes
Bias section absent; detection probability and geographic sampling bias not discussed
License not expressed as a machine-readable SPDX identifier
summary.overall_assessment: The NEON Ground beetles dataset has excellent metadata documentation with strong coverage of methods, quality control, and data structure. The use of schema.org vocabulary and API access makes it highly FAIR-compliant. The main gaps are in attribution (individual contributors and ORCIDs), AI/ML-specific guidance (split strategies, bias documentation, inappropriate use warnings), and several technical details (checksums, file format declarations, software provenance). The extensive change logs demonstrate exceptional transparency in documenting data quality issues and limitations over time.

fair4ai_scores.findable: 9/10 — Persistent identifier, rich metadata, comprehensive keywords; loses one point for absence of a DOI
fair4ai_scores.accessible: 8/10 — API access, free and open, clear license; loses points for undocumented cloud access and non-SPDX license
fair4ai_scores.interoperable: 8/10 — Schema.org and DarwinCore standards used; loses points for missing file format declarations and unlinked controlled vocabulary URIs
fair4ai_scores.reusable: 7/10 — Excellent methods and provenance documentation; loses points for missing attribution, checksums, and AI/ML usage guidance
fair4ai_scores.ai_ready: 6/10 — Strong sampling metadata and annotation provenance; loses points for no split guidance, absent bias section, no software provenance, no AI/ML use history, and no issue reporting channel
